# Importance Sampling

1. Usually employed to approximate expected values w.r.t. a random variable $\theta$ on $\Theta$
$$
\mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p} [h(\theta)]
$$
when $p$ is intractable. E.g., $p(\theta)$ is the posterior distribution of a model

3. Popular in Reinforcement Learning: e.g. "Importance Sampling Techniques for Policy Optimization" by Metelli et al (2020) Journal of Machine Learning Research

4. Can be used also to approximate the intractable distribution $p(\cdot)$

## Example 1 - Standard Gaussian distribution

Let 
$$
    p(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \mathrm{e}^{-\theta^2 / 2} \quad\text{and}\quad q(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma} \mathrm{e}^{-\theta^2 / (2 \sigma^2)}
$$
Let's compare the performance in estimating $\mathbb E_{\theta \sim p}[\theta]$.
```{r}
# First, consider standard Monte Carlo
nrep <- 1000
nsamples <- 100

# Draw standard normal variates (matrix: 1000 rows, 100 columns)
thetas <- matrix(rnorm(nrep * nsamples), nrow = nrep, ncol = nsamples)

# Compute cumulative Monte Carlo averages across rows (samples 1..100)
# Essentially, this operation does the following:
```
$$
  \hat{\theta}_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^j\theta_{ik}}{j}
$$  
This is done because the i-th row represents the evolution of the average at the i-th experiment; the j-th column represents the state of all the experiments' at the j-th step-
```{r}
# apply with margin = 1 operates row-wise; t() transposes back to 1000 X 100
mc_avg <- t(apply(thetas, 1, function(row) cumsum(row) / 1:nsamples))

# Compute mean and standard deviation across iterations (columns)
mean_vec <- colMeans(mc_avg)
sd_vec <- apply(mc_avg, 2, sd)

n_grid <- 1:nsamples

# Base plot line
plot(
  n_grid, mean_vec, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(mean_vec - sd_vec, mean_vec + sd_vec)),
  xlab = "Sample Size (n)", ylab = "Monte Carlo Estimate",
  main = "Monte Carlo Convergence"
)

# Add shaded region 
polygon(
  c(n_grid, rev(n_grid)),
  c(mean_vec - sd_vec, rev(mean_vec + sd_vec)),
  col = rgb(70/255, 130/255, 180/255, 0.3),
  border = NA
)

rate <- 1/sqrt(n_grid)
lines(n_grid, mean_vec, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
lines(n_grid, rate, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
lines(n_grid, -rate, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "darkgray")

```

```{r}
set.seed(123)
nrep <- 1000
nsamples <- 100
sigmas <- c(0.35, sqrt(2)/2, 1, sqrt(2))

# Setup 1 X 4 panel layout
par(mfrow = c(1, length(sigmas)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (sig in sigmas) {
  # Sample from proposal
  thetas <- matrix(rnorm(nrep * nsamples, mean = 0, sd = sig), nrow = nrep, ncol = nsamples)
  
  # Calculate importance weights and weighted samples
  weights <- dnorm(thetas) / dnorm(thetas, mean = 0, sd = sig)
  weighted_thetas <- thetas * weights
  
  # Calculate cumulative averages row-wise
  is_avg <- t(apply(weighted_thetas, 1, function(row) cumsum(row) / 1:nsamples))
  
  # Column-wise mean and standard deviation
  mean_vec <- colMeans(is_avg)
  sd_vec <- apply(is_avg, 2, sd)
  n_grid <- 1:nsamples
  
  plot(
    n_grid, mean_vec, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
    ylim = range(c(mean_vec - sd_vec, mean_vec + sd_vec)),
    xlab = "n", ylab = "IS Estimate", main = paste0("sigma = ", sig)
  )
  
  polygon(
    c(n_grid, rev(n_grid)),
    c(mean_vec - sd_vec, rev(mean_vec + sd_vec)),
    col = rgb(70/255, 130/255, 180/255, 0.3),
    border = NA
  )
  
  lines(n_grid, mean_vec, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
  
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "darkgray")
}

# Reset graphics panel
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Homework**: find the optimal $\sigma$ (it's not 1!)
*Hint*: you have to minimize the variance of the IS estimator.

## Example 2- Importance Sampling for posterior inference on the `VetBP` dataset
$$
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
    y_1, \ldots, y_n \mid \mu, \sigma & \stackrel{\tiny{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \\
    \mu & \sim \mathcal{N}(124, 7.5^2) \\
    \sigma & \sim \text{logN}(\log(13.43), 0.5)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
$$
```{r}
sigrange <- seq(0.01, 100, length.out = 1000)
density_vals <- dlnorm(sigrange, meanlog = log(13.43), sdlog = 0.5)

plot(
  sigrange, density_vals, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
  xlab = expression(sigma), ylab = "Density", main = "Log-Normal Density"
)
```

```{r, include = T}
df <- read.csv("vetbp.csv")
sbp <- df$SBP_00
length(sbp)
```

### The choice of $q$

We are interested in computing expectations w.r.t. $\pi(\mu, \sigma \mid \mathbf{y})$, so $q$ must be a probability on $\mathbb{R} \times [0, +\infty)$

For instance, we could consider $q$ to be the prior!

Let's start with a simple computation of the posterior expected value
$$
    \mathbb{E}[\sigma \mid \mathbf{y}]
$$

```{r}
# Prior sampling function: draws mu ~ Normal, sigma ~ LogNormal
sample_prior <- function(size, mu_mean, mu_std, sig_loc, sig_scale) {
  mu <- rnorm(size, mean = mu_mean, sd = mu_std)
  sigma <- rlnorm(size, meanlog = sig_loc, sdlog = sig_scale)
  
  # Matrix with columns [mu, sigma]
  cbind(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
}

# Normalized Importance Sampling weights 
normalized_is_weights_prior <- function(data, samples) {
  mu_samples <- samples[, 1]
  sigma_samples <- samples[, 2]
  log_lik <- numeric(nrow(samples)) # creates a vector samples-long
  # For each sample w(theta) = L(y | theta) * pi(theta) / q(theta)
  # here pi(theta) = q(theta) because I am using the prior as proposal
  # so w(theta) = L(y | theta)
  for (i in 1:nrow(samples)) {
    log_lik[i] <- sum(dnorm(data, mean = mu_samples[i], sd = sigma_samples[i], log = TRUE))
  }
  
  # Note that we are summing the samples across the data-axis, because we are considering the log-likelihood. It means considering the log-likelihood for each possible choice of mu and sigma
  
  log_weights <- (log_lik)
  
  # We should compute np.exp(weights) / np.sum(np.exp(weights)) --> leads to numerical errors (see also LAB4)
  # Instead, use the "logsumexp" trick
  # https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LogSumExp
  
  max_log <- max(log_weights)
  lse <- max_log + log(sum(exp(log_weights - max_log)))
  
  # Compute normalized weights in probability space
  log_norm_weights <- log_weights - lse # subtracting is like dividing in log-domain
  return(exp(log_norm_weights)) # returning back to "normal" domain
}
```

```{r}
# Generate prior samples (10000 X 2 matrix: [mu, sigma])
samples <- sample_prior(10000, mu_mean = 124, mu_std = 7.5, sig_loc = log(13.43), sig_scale = 0.5)

# Calculate normalized importance weights
weights <- normalized_is_weights_prior(sbp, samples)
# Print sum of weights (should be 1.0)
cat("Sum of weights: ", sum(weights), "\n")

# Calculate posterior mean of sigma (weighted average)
mean_sig <- sum(weights * samples[, 2])
cat("mean_sig: ", mean_sig, "\n")
```

*Is this a good proposal?* We can look at the **effective sample size** (ESS), defined as:
$$
   ESS = \frac{1}{\sum w_i^2}
$$

```{r}
# Compute effective sample size
ess <-  1.0 / sum(weights ^ 2)
cat("ess: ", ess)
```

What if we use a better proposal? For instance, we know the mean really concentrates around the empirical average 

$$
    q(\mu, \sigma) = \mathcal{N}(\mu; 134.5, 10) \times \mathcal{N}(\hat \sigma, 2)
$$

where $\hat \sigma = \frac{1}{n} \sqrt{\sum (y_i - 134.5)^2}$


```{r}
# Proposal sampler: draws mu ~ Normal, sigma ~ Normal
sample_q <- function(size, mu_mean, mu_std, sig_loc, sig_scale) {
  mu    <- rnorm(size, mean = mu_mean, sd = mu_std)
  sigma <- rnorm(size, mean = sig_loc,  sd = sig_scale)
  
  cbind(mu = mu, sigma = sigma)
}

normalized_is_weights_q <- function(data, samples, 
                                    prior_mu_mean, prior_mu_std, 
                                    prior_sig_loc, prior_sig_scale, 
                                    prop_mu_mean, prop_mu_std, 
                                    prop_sig_loc, prop_sig_scale) {
  
  mu_samples    <- samples[, 1]
  sigma_samples <- samples[, 2]
  
  # For each sample w(theta) = L(y | theta) * pi(theta) / q(theta)
  # here pi(theta) != q(theta)
  log_liks <- apply(samples, 1, function(p) {
    if (p[2] <= 0) return(-Inf) # Guard against invalid sigma
    sum(dnorm(data, mean = p[1], sd = p[2], log = TRUE))
  })
  
  print(log_liks)
  
  # mu ~ Normal(prior_mu_mean, prior_mu_std)
  # sigma ~ LogNormal(prior_sig_loc, prior_sig_scale)
  log_prior_mu  <- dnorm(mu_samples, mean = prior_mu_mean, sd = prior_mu_std, log = TRUE)
  log_prior_sig <- suppressWarnings(
    dlnorm(sigma_samples, meanlog = prior_sig_loc, sdlog = prior_sig_scale, log = TRUE)
  )
  log_prior_sig[sigma_samples <= 0] <- -Inf
  log_prior <- log_prior_mu + log_prior_sig
  
  # Compute log-proposal log q(mu, sigma) = q(mu)*q(sigma)
  # mu ~ Normal(prop_mu_mean, prop_mu_std)
  # sigma ~ Normal(prop_sig_loc, prop_sig_scale)
  log_prop_mu  <- dnorm(mu_samples, mean = prop_mu_mean, sd = prop_mu_std, log = TRUE)
  log_prop_sig <- dnorm(sigma_samples, mean = prop_sig_loc, sd = prop_sig_scale, log = TRUE)
  log_prop     <- log_prop_mu + log_prop_sig
  
  log_weights <- log_liks + log_prior - log_prop
  
  # LogSumExp trick for numerical normalization
  valid_idx <- is.finite(log_weights)
  if (!any(valid_idx)) {
    stop("All particle log-weights are non-finite. Check proposal overlap with prior/likelihood.")
  }
  
  max_log <- max(log_weights[valid_idx])
  lse <- max_log + log(sum(exp(log_weights[valid_idx] - max_log)))
  
  weights <- numeric(length(log_weights))
  weights[valid_idx] <- exp(log_weights[valid_idx] - lse)
  
  return(weights)
}
```

```{r}
sigmahat = sqrt(mean((sbp - mean(sbp))^2))
sigmahat
```


```{r}
samples <-  sample_q(10000, 134.5, sqrt(10), sigmahat, sqrt(2))
weights <-  normalized_is_weights_q(sbp, samples, 124, 7.5, log(13.43), 0.5,
                                  134.5, sqrt(10), sigmahat, sqrt(2))
cat("Sum of weights: ", sum(weights), "\n")

mean_mu <- sum(weights * samples[, 1])
cat("mean_mu: ", mean_mu, "\n")
mean_sig <- sum(weights * samples[, 2])
cat("mean_sig: ", mean_sig, "\n")

ess <-  1.0 / sum(weights ^ 2)
cat("ess: ", ess, "\n")
```

**Homework**

Experiment a bit on the proposal distribution. For instance, we could use as proposal $q$ the posterior from the Normal-Inverse Gamma model (which is conjugate and known in closed form).

```{r}
# Proposal sampler: NNIG
sample_nig_q <- function(size, mu_0, lambda, alpha_0, beta_0) {
  sigma_sq <- extraDistr::rinvgamma(size, alpha = alpha_0,  beta = beta_0)
  mu    <- rnorm(size, mean = mu_0, sd = sqrt(sigma_sq/lambda))
  
  cbind(mu = mu, sigma = sqrt(sigma_sq))
}

compute_nig_posterior_parameters <- function(data, mu_0, lambda, alpha_0, beta_0) {
  # Computation of sigma posterior parameters
  avg <- mean(data)
  
  post_alpha <- alpha_0 + length(data)/2
  post_beta <- beta_0 + 0.5 * sum((data - avg)**2) + length(data) * lambda * (avg - mu_0)**2 / (2 * (length(data) + lambda))
  
  # Computation of mu posterior parameters  
  post_mu <- (length(data) * avg + lambda * mu_0) / (length(data) + lambda)
  post_lambda <- length(data) + lambda
  
  return (list(post_alpha = post_alpha, post_beta = post_beta, post_mu = post_mu, post_lambda = post_lambda))
}

normalized_is_nig_weights_q <- function(data, samples, 
                                    prior_mu_mean, prior_mu_std, 
                                    prior_sig_loc, prior_sig_scale, 
                                    prop_mu_0, prop_lambda, 
                                    prop_alpha_0, prop_beta_0) {
  
  mu_samples    <- samples[, 1]
  sigma_samples <- samples[, 2]
  
  # For each sample w(theta) = L(y | theta) * pi(theta) / q(theta)
  # here pi(theta) != q(theta)
  log_liks <- apply(samples, 1, function(p) {
    if (p[2] <= 0) return(-Inf) # Guard against invalid sigma
    sum(dnorm(data, mean = p[1], sd = p[2], log = TRUE))
  })
  
  # mu ~ Normal(prior_mu_mean, prior_mu_std)
  # sigma ~ LogNormal(prior_sig_loc, prior_sig_scale)
  log_prior_mu  <- dnorm(mu_samples, mean = prior_mu_mean, sd = prior_mu_std, log = TRUE)
  log_prior_sig <- suppressWarnings(
    dlnorm(sigma_samples, meanlog = prior_sig_loc, sdlog = prior_sig_scale, log = TRUE)
  )
  log_prior_sig[sigma_samples <= 0] <- -Inf
  log_prior <- log_prior_mu + log_prior_sig
  
  # Compute log-proposal log q(mu, sigma) = log q(mu|sigma) + log q(sigma)
  # 1/sigma ~ Gamma(shape = prop_alpha_0, rate = prop_beta_0)
  # mu | sigma ~ Normal(prop_mu_0, 1/(prop_lambda * sigma))
  log_prop_sig <- extraDistr::dinvgamma(sigma_samples**2, alpha = prop_alpha_0, beta = prop_beta_0, log = TRUE)
  log_prop_mu  <- dnorm(mu_samples, mean = prop_mu_0, sd = sigma_samples/sqrt(prop_lambda), log = TRUE)
  
  log_prop     <- log_prop_mu + log_prop_sig
  log_weights <- log_liks + log_prior - log_prop
  
  # LogSumExp trick for numerical normalization
  valid_idx <- is.finite(log_weights)
  if (!any(valid_idx)) {
    stop("All particle log-weights are non-finite. Check proposal overlap with prior/likelihood.")
  }
  
  max_log <- max(log_weights[valid_idx])
  lse <- max_log + log(sum(exp(log_weights[valid_idx] - max_log)))
  
  weights <- numeric(length(log_weights))
  weights[valid_idx] <- exp(log_weights[valid_idx] - lse)
  
  return(weights)
}
```

```{r}
attach(compute_nig_posterior_parameters(sbp, 134.5, 1, 1, 1))
# post_mu
# post_lambda
# post_alpha
# post_beta
samples <-  sample_nig_q(10000, post_mu, post_lambda, post_alpha, post_beta)
weights <-  normalized_is_nig_weights_q(sbp, samples, 124, 7.5, log(13.43), 0.5,
                                  post_mu, post_lambda, post_alpha, post_beta)
cat("Sum of weights: ", sum(weights), "\n")

mean_mu <- sum(weights * samples[, 1])
cat("mean_mu: ", mean_mu, "\n")
mean_sig <- sum(weights * samples[, 2])
cat("mean_sig: ", mean_sig, "\n")

ess <-  1.0 / sum(weights ^ 2)
cat("ess: ", ess, "\n")
```

## Sampling from the posterior using Importance Sampling

Define 
$$
    \hat \pi(\theta) = \sum_{j=1}^M \tilde w_j \delta_{\theta_j} 
$$

It can be shown that $\hat \pi(\theta) \rightarrow \pi(\theta \mid \mathbf{y})$ (using an appropriate metric/topology)

Therefore given $\hat \pi(\theta)$ we can obtain $N$ samples $\vartheta_1, \ldots, \vartheta_N$ from (approximately) $\pi(\theta \mid \mathbf{y}$) as follows.

For $i=1, \ldots, N$:
1. sample j from the discrete distribution on $\{1, \ldots, M\}$ with weights $\tilde w_1, \ldots, \tilde w_M$
2. let $\vartheta_i = \theta_j$

## Optimal proposal distribution

Given $h(x)$, the proposal distribution that minimizes the variance of the importance sampling estimator is

$$
    q^*(x) = \frac{|h(x)|p(x)}{\int |h(z)| p(z) \mathrm{d} z}
$$

**Proof**:

The variance of the IS estimator is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
    \text{Var}_{\theta \sim q}\left[h(\theta) \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\right] &= 
        \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim q} \left[h(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q(\theta)^2}\right] - \left(\mathbb E_{\theta \sim q} \left[h(\theta) \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\right] \right)^2 \\
        &= \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim q} \left[h(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q(\theta)^2}\right] - \left( \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p}[h(\theta)] \right)^2
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
and observe that the second term does not depend on $q$!

First, we probe a general lower bound for the first term. Using Jensen's inequality, we know that
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim q} \left[h(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q(\theta)^2}\right] \geq \left( \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim q} \left[ |h(\theta)| \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\right] \right)^2 = (\mathbb E_{\theta \sim p} \left[|h(\theta)|\right])^2
\end{equation*}

Now, let us show that the lower bound is achieved when $q = q^*$
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim q^*} \left[h(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q^*(\theta)^2}\right] = 
    \mathbb{E} \left[ h(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{|h(\theta)|^2 p(\theta)^2} \int |h(z)| p(z) \mathrm{d} z \right] = (\mathbb E_{\theta \sim p} \left[|h(\theta)|\right])^2
\end{equation*}


# Rejection Sampling

In the following, we use rejection sampling to sample from the full conditional of $\sigma$ in our model for the analysis of the `VetBP` dataset.

```{r}
# Target unnormalized log-posterior/density for sigma
log_f <- function(sigma, ndata, sumsq) {
  if (sigma <= 0) return(-Inf)
  - (ndata + 1) * log(sigma) - 0.5 / (sigma^2) + sumsq - 
    log(sigma * 0.5) - 0.5 * (log(sigma) - log(13.43))^2
}

# Proposal log-density (Inverse-Gamma)
log_g <- function(sigma, ndata, sumsq) {
  - (ndata + 1) * log(sigma) - 0.5 / (sigma^2) + sumsq
}

# Rejection sampling for full conditional of sigma
sample_fullcond_sigma <- function(data, mu) {
  n <- length(data)
  sumsq <- sum((data - mu)^2)
  
  shape_param <- (n - 1) / 2.0
  rate_param  <- sumsq / 2.0
  
  repeat {
    # Draw from Inverse-Gamma(shape, rate) by inverting a Gamma draw
    gamma_draw <- rgamma(1, shape = shape_param, rate = rate_param)
    prop <- sqrt(1 / gamma_draw)
    
    # Draw uniform acceptance threshold
    u <- runif(1)
    
    # Accept/Reject decision in log-space
    log_alpha <- log_f(prop, n, sumsq) - log_g(prop, n, sumsq)
    
    if (log(u) < log_alpha) {
      return(prop)
    }
  }
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(42)

# Condition on mu = 134 and draw 1000 samples
rej_samps <- replicate(1000, sample_fullcond_sigma(sbp, 134))

hist(
  rej_samps, 
  breaks = 30, 
  col = "steelblue", 
  border = "white",
  xlab = expression(sigma), 
  main = expression("Rejection Sampling Draws for " * sigma * " (" * mu * " = 134)")
)
```

**Homework**

Try to sample from the normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ truncated on [a, b] using rejection sampling. 
As proposal, you can use  $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

What happens when

1. [a, b] is centered around 0 and large (e.g. [-1, 1])
2. [a, b] is centered around 0 and small (e.g. [-0.5, 0.5])
3. [a, b] moves to one of the tail (e.g. consider [$a_n, b_n$] = [-1 + n, 1+n])

```{r}
# Target unnormalized log-posterior/density for x
log_trunc_norm <- function(prop, a, b) {
  if (prop < a) return(-Inf)
  if (prop >= b) return (-Inf)
  log(dnorm(prop))
}


# Rejection sampling for full conditional of x
sample_fullcond_trunc_norm <- function(a, b) {
  i <- 0
  
  repeat {
    # Draw from Standard normal
    i <-  i+1
    prop <- rnorm(1)
    
    # Draw uniform acceptance threshold
    u <- runif(1)
    
    # Accept/Reject decision in log-space
    log_alpha <- log_trunc_norm(prop, a, b) - dnorm(prop, log = TRUE)
    
    if (log(u) < log_alpha) {
      return(c(prop, i))
    }
  }
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(42)

trials <- 1000

# Draw 1000 samples
rej_samps <- replicate(trials, sample_fullcond_trunc_norm(-1, 1))
hist(
  rej_samps[1, ], 
  breaks = 30, 
  col = "steelblue", 
  border = "white",
  xlab = expression(x), 
  main = expression("Rejection Sampling Draws for " * x * ")")
)
print("Proportion of accepted samples:")
print(trials/sum(rej_samps[2, ]))
```
